bibliography: Thompson, Millett Taylor. "Oak Galls." An Illustrated Catalogue of American Insect Galls, edited by E. P. Felt, Rensselaer, 1915.

caption: Wool Sower Wasp Galls, Tisbury, Massachusetts (May 25, 2026).
alt: A photograph of a wool sower gall on a small oak twig beside a tree trunk: a soft, woolly white ball spotted with pink, like a tuft of cotton.
bibliography: Weberling, Ryan. Wool Sower Wasp Galls, Tisbury, Massachusetts. Photograph, 25 May 2026.

caption: “Wool Sower Gall,” from Carl F. Gronemann, Fifty Common Plant Galls of the Chicago Area, Botany Leaflet 16 (Chicago: Chicago Field Museum, 1930), p. 13.
alt: A book page describing the wool sower gall, beside a pen drawing of an oak twig bearing a round, woolly gall, with a single small gall drawn next to it.
bibliography: Gronemann, Carl F. "Wool Sower Gall." Fifty Common Plant Galls of the Chicago Area, Botany Leaflet 16, Field Museum of Natural History, 1930.

caption: “The Pink Moccasin-Flower. (Cypripedium acaule.),” from Grace Greylock Niles, Bog-Trotting for Orchids (New York: The Knickerbocker Press, 1904), colored frontispiece.
alt: A color photograph of pink lady’s slippers growing in a shady wood: several tall stems, each with a single pink, pouch-shaped flower, above broad, ribbed leaves.
bibliography: Niles, Grace Greylock. "The Pink Moccasin-Flower (Cypripedium acaule)." Frontispiece, Bog-Trotting for Orchids, Knickerbocker Press, 1904.

caption: “Cypripedium acaule,” from All of Nature’s Fashions in Lady’s Slippers for the Northern and Eastern Parts of the United States (Boston: Bradlee Whidden, 1885), n.p.
alt: A black-and-white photograph of a single lady’s slipper orchid: one drooping, pouch-shaped flower atop a tall bare stem, above two broad leaves.
bibliography: Young, C. S. "Cypripedium acaule." All of Nature’s Fashions in Lady’s Slippers for the Northern and Eastern Parts of the United States, Bradlee Whidden, 1885.

caption: “The Pink Moccasin-Flower - The Stemless Lady’s Slipper,” from Grace Greylock Niles, Bog-Trotting for Orchids, p. 247.
alt: A color plate of a pink lady’s slipper taken apart: the pink, veined pouch, the long brown-red petals and sepals, and smaller parts laid out in rows.
bibliography: Niles, Grace Greylock. "The Pink Moccasin-Flower – The Stemless Lady’s Slipper." Bog-Trotting for Orchids, Knickerbocker Press, 1904.

caption: Richard William Seale, “The Course of the Solar Maculae over the Sun’s Disk” (n.d.).
alt: An engraved diagram of the sun as a large circle, with rows of numbered dark spots crossing it from east to west to show how the sunspots moved over several days.
bibliography: Seale, Richard William. "The Course of the Solar Maculae over the Sun’s Disk." n.d.

caption: Étienne Léopold Trouvelot, “Plate IV. Solar Prominences.” (Wellcome Collection). Rpt. from Annals of the Astronomical Observatory of Harvard College, Vol. VIII (Cambridge: John Wilson and Son, 1876).
alt: A plate of four strips of drawings, bright red on black, showing solar prominences: flame-like jets, arches and plumes of gas rising from the sun’s edge, with a scale in miles below.
bibliography: Trouvelot, Étienne Léopold. "Plate IV. Solar Prominences." Annals of the Astronomical Observatory of Harvard College, vol. 8, John Wilson and Son, 1876. Wellcome Collection, London.

caption: “Early sunspot drawings from naked-eye observations,” rpt. from R. Arlt and J.M. Vaquero, “Historical sunspot records.” Living Reviews in Solar Physics 17.1 (2020).
alt: Two early drawings of sunspots: a medieval manuscript page with the sun drawn as a circle holding two dark spots, among lines of Latin; and an East Asian painting of a red sun marked with dark spots, above a misty landscape with pines and rocky peaks.
bibliography: Arlt, R., and J. M. Vaquero. "Early Sunspot Drawings from Naked-Eye Observations." "Historical Sunspot Records," Living Reviews in Solar Physics, vol. 17, no. 1, 2020.

caption: “Amelanchier Canadensis,” Plate CXCIV from Charles Sprague Sargent, The Silva of North America, Vol. IV: Rosaceae-Saxifragaceae (Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1892), p. 133.
alt: A botanical engraving of serviceberry: a branch of five-petalled white blossoms and a branch of round berries among oval, finely toothed leaves, with numbered close-ups of the flower and fruit.
bibliography: Sargent, Charles Sprague. "Amelanchier canadensis." Plate CXCIV, The Silva of North America, vol. 4, Houghton Mifflin, 1892.

caption: “Amelanchier arborea (Michx. f.) Fern., downy serviceberry,” from Elbert L. Little Jr., Atlas of United States Trees, Vol. 4: Minor Eastern Hardwoods (Washington, DC: USDA Forest Service, 1976), p. 51.
alt: A map of North America with the downy serviceberry’s range shaded red across the eastern United States and southeastern Canada, from the Great Lakes and New England south to the Gulf states.
bibliography: Little, Elbert L., Jr. "Amelanchier arborea (Michx. f.) Fern., Downy Serviceberry." Atlas of United States Trees, vol. 4, Minor Eastern Hardwoods, USDA Forest Service, 1976.

caption: “Saskatoon Serviceberry: Transverse Section, Radial Section, Tangential Section,” from E.S. Harrar, Hough’s Encyclopaedia of American Woods (New York: Robert Speller & Sons, 1957), specimen 287.
alt: Three color photographs of pale, honey-colored serviceberry wood, each in a green border: the end grain with its growth rings, and two lengthwise cuts showing the straight grain.
bibliography: Harrar, E. S. "Saskatoon Serviceberry: Transverse Section, Radial Section, Tangential Section." Hough’s Encyclopaedia of American Woods, Robert Speller & Sons, 1957.

caption: “Fay’s Prolific,” from Fruit Culture, Volume 2 (Scranton, Pennsylvania: International Textbook Company, 1913), Section 19.
alt: A color painting of red currants: three long, hanging clusters of glossy, translucent red berries on a woody stem among lobed green leaves.
bibliography: "Fay’s Prolific." Fruit Culture, vol. 2, International Textbook Company, 1913.

caption: “Red Dutch. Raceme and detail of flower.” The Red and White Currants. Wooster, Ohio: Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station, 1923.
alt: A photograph of a red currant’s drooping spray of small flowers, beside labelled drawings of a single flower seen from above and cut in half, naming its sepals, petals, stamens, pistil and ovary.
bibliography: "Red Dutch. Raceme and Detail of Flower." The Red and White Currants, Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station, 1923.

caption: “A currant bush before pruning,” Currants and Gooseberries: Their Culture and Relation to White-Pine Blister Rust (Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Agriculture Farmer’s Bulletin 1398, September 1929), p. 10.
alt: A pen drawing of a currant bush before pruning: a crowded fan of long, bare, upright stems rising from the ground.
bibliography: "A Currant Bush before Pruning." Currants and Gooseberries: Their Culture and Relation to White-Pine Blister Rust, Farmers’ Bulletin 1398, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Sept. 1929.

caption: Nasca artist(s), Corn Stalk-Shaped Vessel (c. 1-600 CE).
alt: A ceramic vessel in the shape of a corn stalk, painted dark red with thin cream bands at the joints, with two cream ears of corn, cross-hatched in brown, branching from its sides.
bibliography: Nasca artist(s). Corn Stalk-Shaped Vessel. c. 1–600 CE.

caption: C. Mir, et al. “Out of America: Tracing the Genetic Footprints of the Global Diffusion of Maize.” Theoretical and Applied Genetics [Berlin/Heidelberg] 126.11 (November 2013: 2671–2682), p. 2679.
alt: A world map tracing how maize spread from the Americas, with colored arrows labelled “Spanish,” “Portuguese” and with dates crossing to Europe, Africa and Asia, and colored patches marking where each strain took hold.
bibliography: Mir, C., et al. "Out of America: Tracing the Genetic Footprints of the Global Diffusion of Maize." Theoretical and Applied Genetics, vol. 126, no. 11, Nov. 2013, pp. 2671–2682.

caption: Zea Mays L (1892/1893), from Atlas des plantes de France, Royal Botanic Garden of Madrid.
alt: A color botanical plate of corn: a tall stalk with long green leaves and a tasselled top, and a large ear peeled open to show rows of golden kernels.
bibliography: Zea mays L. 1892/1893. Atlas des plantes de France, Real Jardín Botánico, Madrid.

caption: “Plate XIV,” from George Ashley Crosthwait, Indian Corn (Zea mays): Production, Selection, Preservation, and Germination of Its Seed, and General Principles of Planting (Urbana-Champaign, Illinois: University of Illinois College of Agriculture, 1903).
alt: A sepia photograph of a single tall corn plant posed against a pale backdrop, its leaves drooping and curled, with a few small ears along the stalk.
bibliography: Crosthwait, George Ashley. "Plate XIV." Indian Corn (Zea mays): Production, Selection, Preservation, and Germination of Its Seed, and General Principles of Planting, University of Illinois College of Agriculture, 1903.

caption: “Vaccinium corymbosum: Stanley.” J. Marion Shull, USDA Pomological Watercolor Collection
alt: A watercolor of a cluster of highbush blueberries, round and dusty blue-grey, set alone on a large sheet of cream paper.
bibliography: Shull, J. Marion. "Vaccinium corymbosum: Stanley." USDA Pomological Watercolor Collection, National Agricultural Library.

caption: “Plate XII. Blueberry Propagation Frames.” Frederick V. Coville, Directions for Blueberry Culture. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Bulletin No. 974. Washington, DC: Government Printing Office, 1921.
alt: Two photographs on a book page of blueberry propagation frames: long rows of low wooden cold frames under a timber framework, one shaded with muslin and one with slatted wooden covers.
bibliography: Coville, Frederick V. "Plate XII. Blueberry Propagation Frames." Directions for Blueberry Culture, Bulletin 974, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Government Printing Office, 1921.

caption: An image in the Lectio Terra post “Week 30: Blueberries, Joseph J. White, Inc., Alix Beeston on Ellena Savage”
alt: A seed-catalog advertisement for Whitesbog Blueberries: a painted branch of leaves with two heavy clusters of berries, some still green or pink, beside a panel of text praising the fruit.
bibliography: Joseph J. White, Inc. Whitesbog Blueberries. Joseph J. White, Inc., 1925. National Agricultural Library, U.S. Department of Agriculture.

caption: William Clark, “Asclepias tuberosa. Tuberous Swallow-wort.” From Richard Morris, Flora Conspicua: A Selection of the Most Ornamental Flowering, Hardy, Exotic and Indigenous Trees, Shrubs, and Herbaceous plants, for Embellishing Flower-Gardens and Pleasure-Grounds. London: Longman, 1826.
alt: A hand-colored botanical plate of butterfly weed: a sturdy stem with long, narrow leaves, crowned by a broad flat cluster of bright orange flowers, with drawings of its seed pod and flower parts.
bibliography: Clark, William. "Asclepias tuberosa. Tuberous Swallow-wort." Richard Morris, Flora Conspicua, Longman, 1826.

caption: Craig Holdrege. Shoot development in common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca). Shoots from one colony, drawn to scale (Summer 2007).
alt: Pencil drawings of common milkweed shoots, drawn to scale, from bare spear-shaped tips in mid-May to a tall, leafy plant with buds by early July, each dated.
bibliography: Holdrege, Craig. Shoot Development in Common Milkweed (Asclepias syriaca). Drawing, Summer 2007.

caption: Illustration of the Constellation Sirius, with text. From The Harley Aratus (c. 820-840). Rheims, France. From the British Library, Harley Collection.
alt: A page from a ninth-century manuscript: the dog star, Sirius, drawn as a large dog whose body is made of lines of tiny written text, with a dark blue head ringed by rays, above lines of Latin verse.
bibliography: "Sirius." Illustration with text, The Harley Aratus, c. 820–840, Rheims. British Library, Harley MS 647.

caption: Plate a03507 (May 2, 1899). Marked-up astronomical plate from Arequipa, Peru, featuring Sirius. Harvard College Observatory, StarGlass.
alt: A glass photographic plate of the night sky, pale green-grey, with a dark, blurred disc of light from Sirius on the right and hundreds of faint stars circled and numbered in ink.
bibliography: Harvard College Observatory. Plate a03507, Arequipa, Peru, 2 May 1899. StarGlass.

caption: “It’s Dog Days, But ‘Dog Days’ is Biggest Hoax Yet.” The Tacoma Times [Tacoma, Washington] (August 2, 1909).
alt: A newspaper drawing of a calendar page for August 1909 with a bulldog’s head bursting through its middle, captioned “Dog Days.”
bibliography: "It’s Dog Days, But ‘Dog Days’ Is Biggest Hoax Yet." The Tacoma Times, 2 Aug. 1909.

caption: W.F. Denning. “Positions of the Perseid Radiant Point, July 15, to August 20.” From “The Observed Motion and Duration of the Radiant Point of the Perseids.” Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (December 1901: 161-169). 168.
alt: A star chart, white on black, tracing the moving radiant of the Perseid meteors as a line of small circles, each dated, from mid-July through August, through the constellations Andromeda, Perseus and Cassiopeia.
bibliography: Denning, W. F. "Positions of the Perseid Radiant Point, July 15 to August 20." "The Observed Motion and Duration of the Radiant Point of the Perseids," Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Dec. 1901, pp. 161–169.

caption: W.F. Denning. “Horary number of Perseïds.” From “The August Perseïds, 1877.” The Observatory 1 (September 1877): 164-166.
alt: A printed table of a night’s meteor watch in August 1877, giving the number of Perseids and other meteors seen in each half hour, with notes on the weather.
bibliography: Denning, W. F. "Horary Number of Perseïds." "The August Perseïds, 1877," The Observatory, vol. 1, Sept. 1877, pp. 164–166.

caption: Perseid meteors photo collage (August 10-15, 2011). NASA/MSFC/Meteoroid Environment Office.
alt: A grid of about fifty blue-tinted night-sky photographs, each showing a single bright streak of a Perseid meteor.
bibliography: NASA/MSFC Meteoroid Environment Office. Perseid meteors photo collage, 10–15 Aug. 2011.

caption: “Courd, Courge, Der Kürbiss.” Eugène Grasset and M. P. Verneuil. La plante et ses applications ornementales. Paris, France: Librairie Centrale des Beaux-Arts, 1896. Plate 14.
alt: An Art Nouveau design plate of gourds: orange, bottle-shaped gourds and pale yellow flowers among large green leaves and twining blue tendrils, with matching decorative borders.
bibliography: Grasset, Eugène, and M. P. Verneuil. "Courge." Plate 14, La plante et ses applications ornementales, Librairie Centrale des Beaux-Arts, 1896.

caption: “Fruit Shape of Each of the Eight Cultivar Groups of Cucurbita Pepo. Proximal (stem) end is at top, distal (blossom end at bottom.” Harry S. Paris. “A Proposed Subspecific Classification for Cucurbita-Pepo.” Phytologia 61.3 (November 1986: 133-138), 136.
alt: Outline drawings of the fruit shapes of eight kinds of summer and winter squash, each labelled: round pumpkin, flat scallop, ribbed acorn, curved crookneck, straightneck, vegetable marrow, long cocozelle and zucchini.
bibliography: Paris, Harry S. "Fruit Shape of Each of the Eight Cultivar Groups of Cucurbita pepo." "A Proposed Subspecific Classification for Cucurbita pepo," Phytologia, vol. 61, no. 3, Nov. 1986, pp. 133–138.

caption: “67. 18 Juin 1771.” Antoine Nicolas Duchesne. The Essai sur l’Histoire Naturelle des Courges. 1786. Ed. Harry S. Paris. The Drawings of Antoine Nicolas Duchesne for His Natural History of the Gourds. Paris, France: Publications scientifiques du Muséum, 2007.
alt: A pencil drawing of a single large striped squash lying on its side, its dark rind marked with pale lengthwise bands and speckles, numbered 67.
bibliography: Duchesne, Antoine Nicolas. "67. 18 Juin 1771." The Drawings of Antoine Nicolas Duchesne for His Natural History of the Gourds, edited by Harry S. Paris, Publications scientifiques du Muséum, 2007.

caption: Quegourdes de turquie (left), Quegourdes (centre) and Concombres (right). Paintings from the Grandes Heures d'Anne de Bretagne (1503–1508). Rpt. Harry S. Paris, et al. “First Known Image of Cucurbita in Europe, 1503-1508.” Annals of Botany 98.1 (July 2006): 41-47.
alt: Three painted borders from a French book of hours, each a climbing vine on a gold ground: bottle gourds with orange flowers, a pale gourd with a white flower, and cucumbers with yellow flowers, among snails, butterflies and insects.
bibliography: Quegourdes de Turquie, Quegourdes and Concombres. Grandes Heures d’Anne de Bretagne, 1503–1508. Reproduced in Harry S. Paris et al., "First Known Image of Cucurbita in Europe, 1503–1508," Annals of Botany, vol. 98, no. 1, July 2006, pp. 41–47.

caption: Fede Galizia. Still Life with Apples, Pears, Cucumbers, Figs, Plums, and a Melon (c. 1625-1630).
alt: A still-life painting on a dark ground: a woven basket heaped with pears and apples, a bowl of figs and plums, a cut melon showing its orange flesh, cucumbers and peaches on a wooden ledge.
bibliography: Galizia, Fede. Still Life with Apples, Pears, Cucumbers, Figs, Plums, and a Melon. c. 1625–1630.

caption: Depiction labelled Qawoun (melon, Cucumis melo). From Kitab al-Hasha'ish fi Hayula al-‘Ilaj al-Tibbi (Arabic translation of Dioscorides’ De Materia Medica, edited by Abu ‘Abdallah al-Natili, approx. 990) and copied in Samarqand, 1082. Rpt. Harry S. Paris, et al. “Medieval emergence of sweet melons, Cucumis melo (Cucurbitaceae).” Annals of Botany 110.1 (May 2012): 23-33.
alt: A painting from an Arabic herbal of a melon plant: twining blue-grey stems curving into a symmetrical pattern, with dark lobed leaves and round yellow melons, labelled in Arabic script.
bibliography: "Qawoun (Melon, Cucumis melo)." Kitāb al-Ḥashā’ish fī hayūlā al-‘ilāj al-ṭibbī, copied in Samarqand, 1082. Reproduced in Harry S. Paris et al., "Medieval Emergence of Sweet Melons, Cucumis melo (Cucurbitaceae)," Annals of Botany, vol. 110, no. 1, May 2012, pp. 23–33.

caption: Juan Sánchez Cotán. Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon, and Cucumber (c. 1602)
alt: A still-life painting of a quince and a cabbage hanging on strings in a stone window frame against a black background, with a cut melon, a slice of it and a cucumber on the ledge below.
bibliography: Sánchez Cotán, Juan. Still Life with Quince, Cabbage, Melon, and Cucumber. c. 1602, San Diego Museum of Art.

caption: “[Man Cutting Watermelon]” (c. 1898-1903). Johnson Photography Studio. The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
alt: A trick photograph of a man with a knife standing beside a watermelon taller than he is, cut open to show its spotted flesh, with a huge slice in front.
bibliography: Johnson Photography Studio. [Man Cutting Watermelon]. c. 1898–1903, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

caption: “Images of watermelon drawn from approx. 1385 to 1395.” Harry S. Paris, et al. “Medieval iconography of watermelons in Mediterranean Europe.” Annals of Botany 112.5 (2013): 867-79.
alt: Six medieval manuscript paintings of watermelons: people picking and eating melons among climbing vines, a market scene, and gardens crowded with round fruit.
bibliography: Paris, Harry S., et al. "Images of Watermelon Drawn from approx. 1385 to 1395." "Medieval Iconography of Watermelons in Mediterranean Europe," Annals of Botany, vol. 112, no. 5, 2013, pp. 867–879.

caption: “Rose Coghlan as "The Watermelon," from the series Fancy Dress Ball Costumes (N73) for Duke brand cigarettes” (1889). The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
alt: A cigarette card portrait of the actress Rose Coghlan in costume as “The Watermelon,” wearing a slice of watermelon as a hat and a red collar trimmed with fruit.
bibliography: "Rose Coghlan as ‘The Watermelon,’ from the Series Fancy Dress Ball Costumes (N73) for Duke Brand Cigarettes." 1889, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

caption: Piet Mondrian. Field with Oak Trees at Dusk (1907-1908). Privately held.
alt: An oil painting of a flat field at dusk, with dark, rust-red masses of oak trees under a smoky, brown and violet sky.
bibliography: Mondrian, Piet. Field with Oak Trees at Dusk. 1907–1908. Private collection.

caption: “Map 180-E. northern red oak, Quercus rubra L.” Elbert L. Little, Jr. Atlas of United States Trees, Vol. 1: Conifers and Important Hardwoods. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Agriculture Forest Service, 1971.
alt: A map of the eastern United States with the northern red oak’s range shaded grey, from Minnesota and Nova Scotia south to Arkansas, Alabama and Georgia, missing only the Gulf coast and Florida.
bibliography: Little, Elbert L., Jr. "Map 180-E. Northern Red Oak, Quercus rubra L." Atlas of United States Trees, vol. 1, Conifers and Important Hardwoods, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, 1971.

caption: “Red Oak and The Pigeon of Passage.” Mark Catesby. The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands, Vol. 1. London, England: n.p., 1729-1732. 22.
alt: A hand-colored engraving of a passenger pigeon, grey-blue with a rosy breast, perched on a large, deeply lobed red oak leaf, with acorns below.
bibliography: Catesby, Mark. "Red Oak and the Pigeon of Passage." The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands, vol. 1, 1729–1732.

caption: “Red Oak. Quercus rubra.” From François André Michaux. The North American sylva, or A description of the forest trees of the United States, Canada and Nova Scotia. Paris, France: 1819.
alt: A color engraving of a red oak leaf, large, glossy green and sharply lobed, with two acorns on a twig at its base, one shown cut in half.
bibliography: Michaux, François André. "Red Oak. Quercus rubra." The North American Sylva, or a Description of the Forest Trees of the United States, Canada and Nova Scotia, 1819.

caption: Bertha E. Jaques. Young Leaves and Blossoms of Hickory Tree (c. 1910). Smithsonian American Art Museum.
alt: Two cyanotypes on brown card, white shapes on deep blue: a hickory twig with young, pointed leaflets; and its long, drooping catkins of blossom.
bibliography: Jaques, Bertha E. Young Leaves and Blossoms of Hickory Tree. c. 1910, Smithsonian American Art Museum, Washington, D.C.

caption: Sophia Thoreau. Inscribed hickory leaves in memory of her brother, Henry (1868). Concord Museum.
alt: A dried, golden-brown hickory leaf of five leaflets, each covered in lines of faded handwriting.
bibliography: Thoreau, Sophia. Inscribed hickory leaves in memory of her brother, Henry. 1868, Concord Museum, Concord, Massachusetts.

caption: “Hicoria ovata.” From Charles Sprague Sargent. The Silva of North America, Vol. VII: Lauraceae - Juglandaceae. Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1895.
alt: A botanical engraving of shagbark hickory: a large compound leaf of five toothed leaflets above a pair of round nuts in their husks, with numbered drawings of the nut whole, opened and cut through.
bibliography: Sargent, Charles Sprague. "Hicoria ovata." The Silva of North America, vol. 7, Houghton Mifflin, 1895.

caption: Annual migration of American Robins, created using the National Audubon Society’s Bird Migration Explorer (March 6, 2026).
alt: A silent, 18-second screen recording of Audubon’s migration map running through a year: brown circles marking where American robins are most abundant spread north across the United States and into Canada through spring and summer, then draw back south in autumn, with yellow dots for individually tracked birds moving among them.
bibliography: National Audubon Society. "American Robin: Annual Migration." Bird Migration Explorer. Screen recording, 6 Mar. 2026.

caption: Charles Marville, [Cloud Study, Paris] (1855–56)

caption: Johann Jakob Frey, Dawn on the Pontine Shore (c. 1843)
alt: An oil sketch of a dawn sky over a flat shore: drifts of small violet clouds high up, a band of white, pink-lit cumulus across the middle, and a thin line of low hills on the far horizon.
bibliography: Frey, Johann Jakob. Dawn on the Pontine Shore (Cloud Study). c. 1843, oil on paper mounted on canvas, private collection. Exhibited in True to Nature: Open-Air Painting in Europe, 1780–1870, Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, and Fondation Custodia, Paris (cat. 108).
title: Dawn on the Pontine Shore

caption: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne in Blue and Silver: The Lagoon, Venice (1879–80)
alt: A dark blue-green night painting of the Venetian lagoon: a tall sailing ship at anchor on the left, a bell tower and low buildings on the right with a few lights reflected in the still water, and the dim shapes of gondolas in the foreground.
bibliography: Whistler, James McNeill. Nocturne in Blue and Silver: The Lagoon, Venice. 1879–80, oil on canvas, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (42.302).
title: Nocturne in Blue and Silver: The Lagoon, Venice
